1:
The commentators begin with a practical difficulty rather than a doctrine. Henry states it plainly: a great deal of fine work had been ordered, and the people were to provide the materials, but who should put them into form? Moses was learned in all the learning of the Egyptians, yet he knew not how to engrave or embroider; and the Israelites, having lived all their days in bondage, knew how to make brick and work in clay but had never been brought up to work in gold or cut diamonds, so that goldsmiths and jewellers would have to be made out of masons and bricklayers. Calvin puts the same objection in stronger terms, that the actual difficulty of the work might have overwhelmed Moses and the whole people with despair, since this was no ordinary task on which the most skilful artificers might exercise their ingenuity but a marvellous structure whose pattern had been shown on the mount, and their servile employments in Egypt were such as would extinguish all intellectual vigour and prevent them aspiring to any liberal art. Gill reads the announcement as forestalling exactly that doubt. From it Calvin draws his rule, that those who obediently follow God's voice are never destitute of his aid.

Being called by name is treated as an honour with few parallels. Ellicott says God so calls only those he appoints to some great work, and lists Moses, Samuel and Cyrus. Gill notes that two Targums paraphrase it as called with a good name, and corrects them: the idiom marks singular and personal choice to an office, not the imposing of a name. Both he and Clarke then observe that the name is significant in any case, meaning in the shadow of God, which Clarke glosses as under the especial protection of the Most High and Gill turns typological, since a man so sheltered was set to make things that were themselves shadows of good things to come. Clarke and Ellicott both trace the genealogy through Hur to Judah, Ellicott adding that the grandfather is generally supposed to be the Hur who supported Moses' hands and was left joint regent with Aaron, while cautioning that there is no evidence for this beyond the identity of the name. On the second workman, Calvin finds it unsurprising that the principal should come from Judah but can account for a companion from Dan only by supposing its obscurity the more highly illustrated the grace of God.

What the filling with the Spirit conferred is the section's real question. Gill narrows it at once: not the special graces of the Spirit nor gifts for spiritual service, but ingenuity and skill in manual arts and mechanical operations. Clarke takes the three nouns apart from their roots, wisdom as the compass of mind that judges what is best to be done, understanding as the capacity to distinguish the parts of a work and see how they connect, and knowledge as practical and experimental acquaintance; he then collects pagan witnesses, quoting the Stoic that the seeds of all arts are implanted in us and God draws out the talent from concealment, and the Odyssey on the craftsman taught by Athene who overlays silver with gold. Wesley states the principle in a line, that skill in common employments is the gift of God, who teaches the tradesman as well as the husbandman and must have the praise of it. Calvin faces the apparent contradiction that God puts wisdom into those already wise-hearted, rejects the common solution that special grace merely aids natural ability, and argues instead that whatever grows in us comes from the continued operation of the Spirit, the endowment already given being only the seed. Ellicott distinguishes the two men's spheres, the one general and the other confined to the textile work.
12:
Why the sabbath law is repeated at this point is the first thing several of them settle, and two reach the same answer independently. Keil and Delitzsch say the repetition is in its proper place here because the thought might easily have occurred that it was allowable to omit the keeping of the sabbath while such a work was in hand. Henry gives the same reason at more length: orders had been given that a tabernacle be furnished with all possible expedition, and lest they think the haste required would justify labouring at it on sabbath days, the caution is seasonably inserted, so that though they must hasten the work they must not break the rest. Henry also traces how often the law had already been given, before any other law by way of preparation, then in the body of the moral law as the fourth commandment, then annexed to the judicial law, and now added to the ceremonial, and offers a reason for that pattern: the observance of the sabbath is the hem and hedge of the whole law, standing in the moral law between the two tables, so that where no conscience is made of it, farewell both godliness and honesty.

What the sabbath is a sign of is answered historically by Ellicott and theologically by the rest. Ellicott makes it a replacement: circumcision had been given as the covenant sign to Abraham and his descendants, but its adoption by many heathen nations had left it no longer a distinguishing mark by which God's people could certainly be known, so a new sign was needed; the observance of one day in seven proved effectual because it was not likely to be adopted by the heathen and in fact was not, and it was still regarded as the special badge of a Jew in the latest period of the nation, as the Roman satirists attest. Wesley reads the sign in two directions at once, as a great instance of God's favour in distinguishing them from all other people and as a great instance of their duty in observing it, and adds a claim of his own: by keeping one day in seven they testified that they worshipped the God who made the world in six days, and so distinguished themselves from nations who, having first lost the sabbath and with it the memorial of the creation, by degrees lost the knowledge of the Creator and gave the creature the honour due to him alone.

The death penalty is defended rather than softened. Ellicott calls the enactment new and ties it to the new dignity the day had acquired, since the sabbath-breaker now threw himself out of covenant with God and did what in him lay to throw the whole people out, so that the penalty is in no way surprising but accords with the general spirit of the code; he glosses cutting off as excommunication in fact. Calvin reasons from the severity back to the institution, that we gather the dignity of the mystery from God deeming an apparently light transgression worthy of death, and holds the offence to be no excusable contempt but a professed overthrow of the mark God had set between his people and the heathen; he notes that the prohibition of kindling fire anticipates the glosses the people would have been ready enough to invent. Clarke supplies the procedure, that the magistrates were to examine and the guilty be stoned. On how long the sign was to last they divide: Gill limits the for ever to the end of the Jewish state at the coming of Christ, as with the land and circumcision; Clarke holds the type must continue in force until the antitype come; Ellicott looks past both to the rest that remains for the people of God.
18:
Ellicott makes the closing verse the point the whole preceding design has been running towards, and argues it by nesting the containers one inside another. The court presupposed the tabernacle; the outer chamber was a mere vestibule to the inner; the inner chamber was a receptacle for the ark; and the ark was a chest constructed to contain the two tables. So the delivery of the tables is the termination and crown of the entire conference on the mountain, and putting that treasure into Moses' hands was the first step towards carrying out a design which had been laid down with a view to it. He notes also that the definite article should stand, giving the two tables rather than two, since these are the ones glanced at earlier and distinctly promised before the ascent was made. Calvin sets the same moment in its sequence differently, observing that the voice had already been heard from the fire, the ten commandments delivered, the form of the tabernacle described and the work already finished by the artificers though not yet dedicated, and that Moses was then withdrawn again from the sight and intercourse of men. Gill marks the parting simply, that God ceased to converse with him in that manner and at leaving gave him the tables.

That the writing was not merely commanded but performed is argued at length by Clarke, who strings four passages together: the promise of tables which God says he has written, this verse on the finger of God, the later statement that the tables were the work of God and the writing his writing graven upon them, and the summary that he added no more but wrote them on two tables of stone. He adds a conjecture from a history of knowledge, that this may have been the first writing in alphabetical characters ever exhibited to the world, though marks or hieroglyphics cut in wood and stone had existed before, and he explains the choice of material by the purpose, that the record might be lasting because the testimony was meant for future generations. Wesley makes a distinction Clarke does not, that the stone tables were not prepared by Moses but probably by the ministry of angels, while the writing was by God's will and power immediately, without the use of any instrument. Ellicott declines to go further than the text allows, saying only that the tables were inscribed by some supernatural process not made by human hand, and that the exact nature of that process is not revealed to us.

On how the ten were distributed between the two stones Gill gives the received answer and then his own preference: five commands on each table, or rather four on the first, that being the largest and containing the duty owed to God, and six on the second, which regard the duty of men to one another. He observes that the whole reduces to two, love to God and love to neighbour, and reports with scepticism the Targum that made the tables sapphire from the throne of glory. Wesley gives the same twofold division and explains the name, that they are called tables of testimony because the written law testified the will of God concerning them and would be a testimony against them if they disobeyed. Calvin asks instead why forty days were needed at all, and answers that though the ten commandments comprised the sum of the doctrine, a clearer exposition was required, so that Moses was taken into the sanctuary of heaven to learn what concerned their full understanding, since he could never have reached their genuine meaning had God not been his teacher. From this Calvin draws two conclusions: that the five books were written as God suggested them, and that all true pastors must be disciples, teaching nothing but what they have received.
